screens.title: Upgrade Categories: Patch, Minor, Major
screens.narratorSegment: Upgrades in Fabric come in different flavors and each has different operational implications. Patch releases are typically backward-compatible bug fixes and security patches within the same minor version. They rarely require configuration changes and are the least disruptive. Minor or major upgrades, such as moving from a 2.2 to a 2.5 line, may introduce new features, A P I changes or changes to channel capabilities. Those upgrades can require a coordinated process: component binaries updated, then channel capabilities updated after components can support them. The practical difference matters: for patch releases you can often update images quickly, but for minor or major upgrades you must plan a sequence that includes testing, possibly updating core. yaml or orderer. yaml, and updating channel configuration in a controlled step after components are at the required level. A common misconception is to treat all upgrades the same; doing so risks enabling a capability before every node supports it, which can break consensus or endorsement behaviour. As an example, imagine a new endorsement policy feature that requires channel capability X — enabling it before all peers and orderers are on the supporting version would produce errors. The key takeaway is to assess whether an upgrade is purely patch or requires capability changes, and then expand your plan accordingly, including backups, staging and rollback options.

keyIdea.title: Release types
keyIdea.text: Patch releases are low risk; minor/major upgrades may require channel capability updates and more careful sequencing.

content.html:
Definition
Patch vs Minor/Major
Patch release
  • Bug fixes and security patches within same minor line.
  • Usually backward-compatible and lower operational impact.
  • Can often be applied quickly with rolling updates.
Common misconception
Assuming patches never require testing. They still require validation, especially on production networks.
Minor / Major upgrade
  • May add features or change behavior and require channel capability updates.
  • Requires staged testing, configuration updates, and coordinated rollouts.
  • Plan for backups and possible data migration steps.
Why it matters
Enabling a new capability before all nodes support it can cause transaction failures or consensus issues.

screens.title: Rolling Upgrade Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A rolling upgrade is an operational pattern where you update subset(s) of nodes one at a time or in small batches, observing health and readiness before proceeding. The advantage is continuous service: peers and orderers remain available because other replicas continue processing transactions. In Fabric, rolling upgrades rely on redundancy — multiple peers per org and a multi-node ordering service like Raft. A typical sequence for an Orderer Raft cluster is: take down one node, upgrade its binaries or container image, bring it back, ensure it rejoins the cluster, then proceed to the next node. For Peers, upgrade each peer that hosts endorsing chaincode, verify endorsement responses, and monitor chaincode commit status across the channel. Important checkpoints during a rolling upgrade include verifying ledger replication, ensuring ledger state DB is available, and confirming peers rejoin with correct MSP/crypto material. A frequent error is updating too many nodes at once or not waiting for readiness, which can reduce quorum and cause service interruptions. Also, remember to update configuration files such as core. yaml only if compatible with the new version. The practical takeaway: plan an ordered sequence, monitor readiness, and escalate rollback when health checks fail.

keyIdea.title: Rolling upgrades
keyIdea.text: Upgrade nodes incrementally, verify rejoin and health, and preserve quorum to avoid service interruption.

content.html:
Process Flow
Node-by-node sequencing
Rolling upgrade steps
  1. Prepare backup and staging validation.
  2. Take one node out of service and upgrade it.
  3. Wait for node to rejoin and confirm health.
  4. Proceed to the next node only after checks pass.
Checkpoints
ledger replication, endorsement responses, ordering quorum
Scenario card
In a 3-node Raft cluster, update the first node and wait for it to rejoin before updating the second. This preserves quorum and keeps ordering service available.
Key Takeaway

Sequence and readiness checks are the safety valves in a rolling upgrade.

screens.title: Kubernetes StatefulSets and Rollouts
screens.narratorSegment: Kubernetes can automate much of the rolling update work for Fabric when components are deployed with StatefulSets or Deployments. StatefulSets are commonly used for Orderers and sometimes Peers because they preserve stable network identity and persistent volumes. When you update the container image field in a StatefulSet manifest and apply it, Kubernetes performs a pod-by-pod replacement: it terminates a pod, starts a new one with the updated image, waits for readiness, and then moves to the next. This behavior aligns with the rolling upgrade strategy: one node upgraded and verified at a time. For Deployments, Kubernetes ensures the desired number of replicas but does not preserve identities; this suits stateless or horizontally scaled services. A critical operational detail is ensuring your manifests include readiness probes and appropriate replica counts so Kubernetes will not take down too many pods at once. The key misconception to avoid is expecting Kubernetes alone to handle Fabric-level health; Kubernetes will ensure pods are running, but cluster-level conditions like ordering quorum or ledger sync must be validated at the application level. Integrate Kubernetes rollout with Fabric health checks and scripted verification to ensure safe progress.

content.html:
Architecture
StatefulSets vs Deployments
StatefulSet behavior
Kubernetes updates Pods one at a time, preserving stable identities and attached persistent volumes, which is useful for Raft Orderers and storage-backed Peers.
Deployment behavior
Deployments scale stateless components and update replicas but do not guarantee stable identities, making them suitable for auxiliary services.
Operational note
Kubernetes readiness probes plus Fabric-level checks are required to confirm a pod is truly ready to serve as a Peer or Orderer.
Practical example
Update the StatefulSet image, apply the manifest, then wait for each pod to become ready and for ordering quorum to be preserved before proceeding.

screens.title: Pre-Upgrade Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Before you start any upgrade you must prepare. A robust checklist reduces surprises and shortens recovery time. First, perform a full backup: ledger data, state database snapshots, and crypto material. Backups are your primary rollback safety net. Second, test the full upgrade end-to-end in a staging environment that mirrors production topology and data where feasible. Third, read the release notes carefully to identify breaking changes or required configuration updates to core. yaml, orderer. yaml, or channel capabilities. Fourth, prepare manifests or images and ensure versioned artifacts — for chaincode, capture the package ID; for container images, tag them immutably. Fifth, communicate a maintenance window to stakeholders and prepare monitoring and logs aggregation for immediate visibility. Sixth, define your rollback plan, including the steps to restore backups if needed. A common misconception is to assume a tested script will run identically in production; differences in traffic, data volume, and timing can expose new issues. The final practical step is to stage the upgrade with a small subset of nodes first to validate assumptions before a broader rollout. Pre-Upgrade Checklist means backups, staging tests, reading release notes, immutable artifacts, and a clear rollback plan are non-negotiable before upgrades.. In practical terms, essential steps before touching production components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Chaincode Lifecycle (v2.x)
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric's v2. x chaincode lifecycle standardizes how chaincode versions are introduced to a channel. It separates packaging and installation from policy approval, ensuring that organizations consent to new definitions before they become active. The lifecycle consists of four main steps. First, package the new chaincode version into an archive with an incremented version label. Packaging produces a package ID used in later steps. Second, install that package on each relevant peer where endorsement is expected. Installation makes the package available locally and yields the package ID. Third, each organization that endorses transactions for that chaincode must approve the new chaincode definition for the channel. Approval includes the version, package ID, sequence number and any endorsement policy changes. Fourth, when enough organizations have approved per the channel's lifecycle policy, a commit operation records the new definition to the channel, making it active for new transactions. A common misconception is that installing on peers alone activates the chaincode; in v2. x, installation is necessary but not sufficient — approvals and commit are required. The lifecycle supports coexistence: old and new versions can both be installed until commit, which enables smooth transition and verification before fully switching over.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle summary
keyIdea.text: Install is local; approval is organizational consent; commit makes the new definition active on the channel.

content.html:
Core Concept
Lifecycle steps
  1. Package: create a versioned archive.
  2. Install: place the package on endorsing peers.
  3. Approve: each org approves the new definition.
  4. Commit: commit the definition to the channel.
Coexistence
Old and new packages can coexist; commit controls which version new transactions use.
Analogy
Think of installation as uploading, approval as governance sign-off, and commit as publishing.

screens.title: Packaging and Installing Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging and installing a new chaincode version is a practical, repeatable process. Begin by updating your chaincode source and version labels and then run the packaging command to produce a tarball. The package command bundles source and metadata into a deterministic archive. After packaging, install the package on each endorsing peer. The peer lifecycle install output includes a package ID — record this value because it is required during approval. Verify installation by running the queryinstalled command which lists installed packages per peer. A common mistake is to forget to capture the package ID or to rely on a locally built image without consistent labeling. If you lose the package ID you must re-run the install or otherwise recover the exact package digest. In practice you should script packaging and installation to reduce manual errors and to ensure the same package ID is used across peers. Below is a visual code panel with the exact commands you will run in the activity; copy and paste them into a properly configured CLI environment when performing the upgrade. Packaging and Installing Chaincode means always capture and record the chaincode package id after install — it's required by approval and commit steps.. In practical terms, create the package and install on peers; capture the package id. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Package command
peer lifecycle chaincode package basic_asset_transfer_v1.1.tar.gz --path /opt/gopath/src/github.com/chaincode/basic-asset-transfer/go --lang golang --label basic_asset_transfer_v1.1

screens.title: Approve, Check Readiness, and Commit
screens.narratorSegment: Approval and commit are governance steps that ensure organizations consent to a new chaincode definition. After installing and recording the package ID, each organization that previously approved the older definition must run the approveformyorg command, supplying the name, version, package ID and an incremented sequence number. The sequence number reflects the definition revision and must increase relative to the prior committed sequence. After approvals, you can run checkcommitreadiness to see which organizations have approved; this helps coordinate multi-org rollouts. Finally, once enough approvals match the channel's lifecycle policy, a single organization commits the new definition with the commit command, which includes peer addresses and TLS root cert files so the orderer can validate endorsements. A common mistake is forgetting to increment the sequence number or mismatching the --init-required flag relative to the prior definition; this can cause the commit to fail. Carefully record flags and use waitForEvent when available to get confirmation. The commands below match the steps you will perform in the hands-on activity. Approve, Check Readiness, and Commit means each org must approve the new definition; use checkcommitreadiness before commit and ensure sequence is incremented.. In practical terms, approve the definition from each organization and commit when ready. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Coexistence: Old & New Chaincode Versions
screens.narratorSegment: One of Fabric v2. x's strengths is that old and new chaincode versions can coexist during the upgrade. Installation places packages on peers without changing the active definition; approval and commit are the governance steps that switch which definition is active for new transactions. This means you can install the new package across peers, run tests invoking the new code in isolated ways, and only commit when confident. If your change is additive and backward-compatible, the transition is usually smooth. However, if you change the data model — for example adding fields or renaming asset keys — you must consider migration logic. Coexistence does not automatically migrate stored data; both versions may read the same ledger format and must cope with legacy records. A common misconception is that committing the new definition instantly migrates data; it does not. Instead, write explicit migration paths in chaincode, such as conditional checks that detect an older schema and transform it on first access. The practical approach is to stage installation, run compatibility tests, commit, and then gradually exercise new functions while monitoring for errors.

Comparison
Before commit
New package installed on peers but channel still uses old committed definition for new transactions.
After commit
New definition is active; new transactions will use the new chaincode version while old binaries may still be present until you deprecate them.

If schema changes, implement in-chaincode migration checks or migration scripts that transform legacy records safely.
Test strategy

screens.title: Data Migration inside Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: When your chaincode upgrades include data model changes you must plan migration steps carefully. Fabric does not automatically rewrite ledger entries; ledger keys and values remain as created until a transaction modifies them. One safe pattern is defensive code: on read, check whether the asset matches the new schema and, if not, transform it to the new format and write it back in the same transaction. This approach migrates data lazily as assets are accessed, avoiding bulk offline migrations that can be risky under load. Another pattern is an explicit migration transaction that iterates over affected keys and rewrites them in a controlled maintenance window; this provides visibility and batching control but must be idempotent and monitor progress. Avoid assumptions that all peers will see the migration at the same instant — design migration logic to be resilient to partial progress. A misconception to guard against is performing migrations without backups or idempotency; if a migration partially completes and fails, restoring a consistent state can be challenging. The takeaway is to design migration logic that is safe, testable and reversible where possible.

Definition
Lazy migration
Detect old schema on read, transform record to new schema, and write update in the same transaction.
Explicit migration
Run controlled migration transactions that iterate keys and update them with idempotency and progress logging.
Safety practices
Back up ledger, test migrations in staging, and ensure idempotent steps to recover from partial runs.
Analogy
Think of lazy migration like gradual in-place upgrades, and explicit migration like a database migration script run during maintenance.

screens.title: Common Challenges and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Upgrades bring both operational risk and opportunity. The most common challenges are unexpected downtime, backward compatibility issues, channel capability mismatches, insufficient monitoring, and lacking rollback procedures. Rolling upgrades reduce downtime but do not remove it entirely; you should anticipate brief periods of reduced capacity or increased latency and plan accordingly. Backward compatibility must be checked across client SDKs and chaincode APIs; sometimes clients need updates to use new features even if the network components are upgraded. Channel capabilities require special attention: only enable new capabilities after all relevant components are upgraded and compatible. Monitoring is vital — track ordering latency, endorsement failures, and peer sync states during and after the upgrade. Finally, a documented rollback plan tied to your backups is essential. Best practices include automated scripts for packaging and install, capturing package IDs and sequence numbers in a controlled way, performing staged rollouts in staging and canary pods, and running post-upgrade verifications. Remember that upgrades are team operations: communicate schedules, responsible owners, and clear decision points for rollback. The practical goal is to reduce mean time to detect and mean time to recover when something goes wrong.

screens.title: Activity: Perform a Chaincode Upgrade

fullNarratorScript:
Upgrades are a routine but mission-critical part of running Hyperledger Fabric. In this lesson you will learn why upgrades matter, what can change between patch, minor and major releases, and how to keep your network stable while bringing in new features. We focus on two parallel upgrade streams: the platform components — Peers, Orderers, and CAs — and chaincode, which follows Fabric's v2. x lifecycle. You will see a practical, low-risk pattern: rolling upgrades that update nodes in small batches so the network remains available. We also cover Kubernetes as an orchestration ally, how to package and approve a new chaincode version, and the importance of a backup, staging tests, and a rollback plan. A short example will show the chaincode lifecycle steps you would run in a CLI. By the end you should be comfortable planning an upgrade window, using StatefulSets or Deployments to perform a controlled rollout, and carrying out a chaincode version change through package, install, approve, and commit. Think about your last maintenance window: what steps would you add now to reduce risk and speed recovery?

In this chapter you will build specific upgrade skills that are essential for operating Fabric in production. First, you'll learn to distinguish patch, minor and major upgrades and understand the implications for channel capabilities and compatibility. Second, you'll practice planning and executing a rolling upgrade so Peers and Orderers remain available while getting updated. Third, you'll implement the Fabric v2. x chaincode lifecycle: packaging, installing, approving, and committing a new definition across organizations. Finally, you will identify and mitigate common upgrade pitfalls — from data migration needs to monitoring and rollback planning — and apply Kubernetes primitives such as StatefulSets and Deployments to make rollouts predictable. Each objective is framed so you can both reason about risk and execute the commands or manifests required in a controlled way. You'll leave with testable checkpoints and a checklist to follow during real maintenance windows.

This second objectives slide focuses on actionable operations and Kubernetes integration. You will learn to map Fabric roles to Kubernetes objects — for example using StatefulSets for Orderers or Peers when stable identity and ordered pod replacement matters, and how Deployments can manage stateless components. You'll also practice how to validate an upgrade in staging, capture package IDs during chaincode install, and increment sequence numbers correctly when approving a new definition. The goal is for you to be comfortable reading a StatefulSet manifest and understanding how a change to an image field produces a controlled pod-by-pod rollout. You'll also plan monitoring checkpoints and a communication strategy for teams during a maintenance window. These competencies let you automate safer upgrades and reduce manual error when updating a live Fabric network. Practical skills and Kubernetes integration means use statefulsets for ordered, identity-preserving updates and deployments for stateless components; test in staging and capture package ids and sequence numbers during chaincode upgrades.. In practical terms, apply kubernetes features to control rollouts and reduce risk. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Upgrades in Fabric come in different flavors and each has different operational implications. Patch releases are typically backward-compatible bug fixes and security patches within the same minor version. They rarely require configuration changes and are the least disruptive. Minor or major upgrades, such as moving from a 2.2 to a 2.5 line, may introduce new features, A P I changes or changes to channel capabilities. Those upgrades can require a coordinated process: component binaries updated, then channel capabilities updated after components can support them. The practical difference matters: for patch releases you can often update images quickly, but for minor or major upgrades you must plan a sequence that includes testing, possibly updating core. yaml or orderer. yaml, and updating channel configuration in a controlled step after components are at the required level. A common misconception is to treat all upgrades the same; doing so risks enabling a capability before every node supports it, which can break consensus or endorsement behaviour. As an example, imagine a new endorsement policy feature that requires channel capability X — enabling it before all peers and orderers are on the supporting version would produce errors. The key takeaway is to assess whether an upgrade is purely patch or requires capability changes, and then expand your plan accordingly, including backups, staging and rollback options.

A rolling upgrade is an operational pattern where you update subset(s) of nodes one at a time or in small batches, observing health and readiness before proceeding. The advantage is continuous service: peers and orderers remain available because other replicas continue processing transactions. In Fabric, rolling upgrades rely on redundancy — multiple peers per org and a multi-node ordering service like Raft. A typical sequence for an Orderer Raft cluster is: take down one node, upgrade its binaries or container image, bring it back, ensure it rejoins the cluster, then proceed to the next node. For Peers, upgrade each peer that hosts endorsing chaincode, verify endorsement responses, and monitor chaincode commit status across the channel. Important checkpoints during a rolling upgrade include verifying ledger replication, ensuring ledger state DB is available, and confirming peers rejoin with correct MSP/crypto material. A frequent error is updating too many nodes at once or not waiting for readiness, which can reduce quorum and cause service interruptions. Also, remember to update configuration files such as core. yaml only if compatible with the new version. The practical takeaway: plan an ordered sequence, monitor readiness, and escalate rollback when health checks fail.

Kubernetes can automate much of the rolling update work for Fabric when components are deployed with StatefulSets or Deployments. StatefulSets are commonly used for Orderers and sometimes Peers because they preserve stable network identity and persistent volumes. When you update the container image field in a StatefulSet manifest and apply it, Kubernetes performs a pod-by-pod replacement: it terminates a pod, starts a new one with the updated image, waits for readiness, and then moves to the next. This behavior aligns with the rolling upgrade strategy: one node upgraded and verified at a time. For Deployments, Kubernetes ensures the desired number of replicas but does not preserve identities; this suits stateless or horizontally scaled services. A critical operational detail is ensuring your manifests include readiness probes and appropriate replica counts so Kubernetes will not take down too many pods at once. The key misconception to avoid is expecting Kubernetes alone to handle Fabric-level health; Kubernetes will ensure pods are running, but cluster-level conditions like ordering quorum or ledger sync must be validated at the application level. Integrate Kubernetes rollout with Fabric health checks and scripted verification to ensure safe progress.

Before you start any upgrade you must prepare. A robust checklist reduces surprises and shortens recovery time. First, perform a full backup: ledger data, state database snapshots, and crypto material. Backups are your primary rollback safety net. Second, test the full upgrade end-to-end in a staging environment that mirrors production topology and data where feasible. Third, read the release notes carefully to identify breaking changes or required configuration updates to core. yaml, orderer. yaml, or channel capabilities. Fourth, prepare manifests or images and ensure versioned artifacts — for chaincode, capture the package ID; for container images, tag them immutably. Fifth, communicate a maintenance window to stakeholders and prepare monitoring and logs aggregation for immediate visibility. Sixth, define your rollback plan, including the steps to restore backups if needed. A common misconception is to assume a tested script will run identically in production; differences in traffic, data volume, and timing can expose new issues. The final practical step is to stage the upgrade with a small subset of nodes first to validate assumptions before a broader rollout. Pre-Upgrade Checklist means backups, staging tests, reading release notes, immutable artifacts, and a clear rollback plan are non-negotiable before upgrades.. In practical terms, essential steps before touching production components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fabric's v2. x chaincode lifecycle standardizes how chaincode versions are introduced to a channel. It separates packaging and installation from policy approval, ensuring that organizations consent to new definitions before they become active. The lifecycle consists of four main steps. First, package the new chaincode version into an archive with an incremented version label. Packaging produces a package ID used in later steps. Second, install that package on each relevant peer where endorsement is expected. Installation makes the package available locally and yields the package ID. Third, each organization that endorses transactions for that chaincode must approve the new chaincode definition for the channel. Approval includes the version, package ID, sequence number and any endorsement policy changes. Fourth, when enough organizations have approved per the channel's lifecycle policy, a commit operation records the new definition to the channel, making it active for new transactions. A common misconception is that installing on peers alone activates the chaincode; in v2. x, installation is necessary but not sufficient — approvals and commit are required. The lifecycle supports coexistence: old and new versions can both be installed until commit, which enables smooth transition and verification before fully switching over.

Packaging and installing a new chaincode version is a practical, repeatable process. Begin by updating your chaincode source and version labels and then run the packaging command to produce a tarball. The package command bundles source and metadata into a deterministic archive. After packaging, install the package on each endorsing peer. The peer lifecycle install output includes a package ID — record this value because it is required during approval. Verify installation by running the queryinstalled command which lists installed packages per peer. A common mistake is to forget to capture the package ID or to rely on a locally built image without consistent labeling. If you lose the package ID you must re-run the install or otherwise recover the exact package digest. In practice you should script packaging and installation to reduce manual errors and to ensure the same package ID is used across peers. Below is a visual code panel with the exact commands you will run in the activity; copy and paste them into a properly configured CLI environment when performing the upgrade. Packaging and Installing Chaincode means always capture and record the chaincode package id after install — it's required by approval and commit steps.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The sequence number reflects the definition revision and must increase relative to the prior committed sequence. After approvals, you can run checkcommitreadiness to see which organizations have approved; this helps coordinate multi-org rollouts. Finally, once enough approvals match the channel's lifecycle policy, a single organization commits the new definition with the commit command, which includes peer addresses and TLS root cert files so the orderer can validate endorsements. A common mistake is forgetting to increment the sequence number or mismatching the --init-required flag relative to the prior definition; this can cause the commit to fail. Carefully record flags and use waitForEvent when available to get confirmation. The commands below match the steps you will perform in the hands-on activity. Avoid assumptions that all peers will see the migration at the same instant — design migration logic to be resilient to partial progress. A misconception to guard against is performing migrations without backups or idempotency; if a migration partially completes and fails, restoring a consistent state can be challenging. The takeaway is to design migration logic that is safe, testable and reversible where possible.

Upgrades bring both operational risk and opportunity. The most common challenges are unexpected downtime, backward compatibility issues, channel capability mismatches, insufficient monitoring, and lacking rollback procedures. Rolling upgrades reduce downtime but do not remove it entirely; you should anticipate brief periods of reduced capacity or increased latency and plan accordingly. Backward compatibility must be checked across client SDKs and chaincode APIs; sometimes clients need updates to use new features even if the network components are upgraded. Channel capabilities require special attention: only enable new capabilities after all relevant components are upgraded and compatible. Monitoring is vital — track ordering latency, endorsement failures, and peer sync states during and after the upgrade. Finally, a documented rollback plan tied to your backups is essential. Best practices include automated scripts for packaging and install, capturing package IDs and sequence numbers in a controlled way, performing staged rollouts in staging and canary pods, and running post-upgrade verifications. Remember that upgrades are team operations: communicate schedules, responsible owners, and clear decision points for rollback. The practical goal is to reduce mean time to detect and mean time to recover when something goes wrong.
